strengths: The paper makes a useful empirical contribution to stereo matching: a procedural dataset recipe combining realistic backgrounds, floating objects, and varied scene types. Its originality lies in systematically adapting and studying existing generators for stereo, rather than introducing a new network.

The strongest evidence is the same-architecture comparison. In Table 3, DLNR trained on Infinigen-Stereo reduces Middlebury 2014 half-resolution error from 5.21 to 3.76 and Booster error from 12.17 to 9.09 versus training on four synthetic datasets combined, while matching ETH3D and improving both KITTI results. Table 4 also shows consistent gains over individual training datasets.

The parameter study provides actionable findings. Table 1 shows substantial benefits from adding floating objects and retaining background furniture; Table 2 demonstrates complementary benefits from mixing scene types. These experiments help explain dataset effectiveness beyond reporting a stronger final benchmark result.

Practical usefulness is supported by results with both RAFT-Stereo and DLNR, the sample-efficiency study in Figure 6, and explicit generation-cost measurements. Reducing rendering time from 3.37 minutes to 27 seconds per frame makes the proposed pipeline substantially more accessible.

Overall, the magnitude and consistency of the controlled dataset comparisons provide a stronger case for acceptance than rejection, despite reservations about evaluation independence and the strength of some explanatory claims.
weaknesses: The main limitation is benchmark-guided dataset selection: the same benchmark sets inform generation choices in Tables 1–2 and support the final generalization claims in Tables 3–4. This remains zero-shot in the stated sense of no target-domain fine-tuning, but does not constitute an independent evaluation of unseen-domain generalization. No quantitative benchmark is clearly reserved from generator development.

The ablations use newly generated 5,000-pair datasets and single reported training runs, without uncertainty estimates or an explicit matched-scene protocol. Consequently, small differences, especially for lighting and object diversity, cannot confidently be attributed to the manipulated parameter. The assertion that these short RAFT-Stereo experiments represent full-scale training is also not directly validated.

Several interpretations exceed the experimental controls. Removing background furniture changes geometry, density, and occlusion as well as realism, so its benefit does not isolate realistic arrangement as the cause. Likewise, high errors on particular materials do not establish that retaining those materials degrades diffuse-region performance; a direct removal ablation and material-stratified evaluation are absent.

Reproduction and comparison details are incomplete. The manuscript relies on original authors' default training settings without enumerating the actual configurations, and does not clearly specify the sampling weights and training schedule for the important DLNR-Mixed baseline. Section 3.2 omits the ETH3D error threshold and describes KITTI using a 3-pixel threshold without clarifying its relationship to the official relative-error criterion.

Some conclusions need narrower wording. Figure 6 establishes sample efficiency only on Middlebury half-resolution EPE. The statement that small stereo baselines worsen every benchmark contradicts Table 1, where ETH3D improves from 3.92 to 2.89. These are correctable reporting issues rather than reasons to discount the main dataset gains.

strengths: The paper makes a useful empirical contribution to synthetic stereo data design. Its main value is the systematic investigation of generation choices and an effective procedural recipe, rather than a new stereo architecture. Tables 1–2 examine object density, backgrounds, materials, camera baselines, rendering quality, and scene mixtures.

The strongest evidence is the controlled dataset comparison. With DLNR trained for 200k steps, Infinigen-Stereo outperforms each alternative dataset across every reported metric in Table 4. Against the stronger mixed-dataset baseline in Table 3, Middlebury-H error falls from 5.21 to 3.76 and Booster error from 12.17 to 9.09, while ETH3D performance is maintained.

The findings have practical relevance beyond a single benchmark. Evaluation covers indoor, outdoor, driving, and challenging reflective scenes, and the final dataset produces strong results with both DLNR and RAFT-Stereo. Figure 6 additionally supports improved sample efficiency on Middlebury.

The generation-cost analysis strengthens the practical contribution: rendering time decreases from 3.37 minutes to 27 seconds per frame, and indoor scene generation from 50.85 to 13 minutes. The appendix provides useful generation and annotation details. Taken together, the demonstrated gains and reusable procedural approach favor acceptance despite the reservations below.
weaknesses: The principal evaluation concern is repeated benchmark-guided generator selection. Section 3 chooses generation settings using the same benchmarks subsequently used to establish final generalization performance. This remains zero-shot in the stated sense of no real-data fine-tuning, but it is not an untouched assessment of target-domain generalization. No separate quantitative benchmark is reserved to measure transfer after these design decisions.

The ablations provide stronger evidence for useful recipes than for the proposed causal explanations. Adding background furniture changes geometry, occlusion, and image statistics alongside realism, so its benefit does not isolate realistic arrangement as the cause. Likewise, Figure 4 identifies high-error materials and objects, but no before/after removal experiment establishes that excluding them improves diffuse-region performance.

The parameter study uses newly generated 5,000-pair datasets and single reported training runs, without uncertainty estimates or an explicit matched-scene protocol. Consequently, small differences, particularly for lighting and object types, cannot confidently be attributed to the tested variable. The claim that these short RAFT-Stereo experiments represent full-scale training is not directly validated through repeated ablations at that scale or with DLNR.

Reproducibility of the strongest baseline is incomplete: the sampling proportions for DLNR-Mixed are not specified, although scene-mixture weighting is explicitly optimized for the proposed data. Training is largely described through references to default settings, and the dark-frame filtering threshold is omitted. These omissions matter for reproducing the dataset comparison and final generated distribution.

Some conclusions need narrower wording. Section 6's baseline discussion says small baselines perform worse across all benchmarks, although Table 1 shows better ETH3D performance (2.89 versus 3.92). Figure 6 supports sample-efficiency claims only on Middlebury-H, and the broad state-of-the-art language should be bounded by the evaluated checkpoints. These are presentation and scope issues rather than reasons to dismiss the substantial measured gains.

strengths: The paper makes a useful empirical contribution to stereo matching by systematically studying procedural training-data design. Its novelty lies in the controlled investigation and effective generation recipe, rather than a new architecture. The findings on floating-object density, realistic backgrounds, camera baselines, and scene mixtures provide actionable guidance.

The strongest evidence is the comparison using the same DLNR architecture. In Table 3, Infinigen-Stereo reduces Middlebury 2014 half-resolution error from 5.21 to 3.76 and Booster error from 12.17 to 9.09 relative to training on four existing synthetic datasets combined, while also improving KITTI performance and matching ETH3D performance. Table 4 further shows consistent gains over individual training datasets.

The contribution extends beyond a single model or benchmark: final training experiments cover RAFT-Stereo and DLNR, with evaluation across indoor, outdoor, driving, and challenging-material datasets. Figure 6 also provides compelling evidence of sample efficiency, although that experiment uses only Middlebury half-resolution EPE.

The computational improvements make the generator more practical. The paper reports reducing indoor scene generation from 50.85 to 13 minutes and rendering from 3.37 minutes to 27 seconds per frame, with downstream evaluation of the rendering trade-off. The appendix documents scene construction, annotations, resolution, and asset types.

Overall, the substantial improvements against a strong combined-data baseline and the reusable dataset-design insights support acceptance. The reservations primarily limit the strength of the generalization and causal claims rather than negate the demonstrated utility.
weaknesses: The same real-world benchmarks guide generator choices in Section 3 and assess the final system in Section 4. Although training uses only synthetic images, the recipe is selected using target-benchmark performance. No clearly untouched quantitative evaluation is reported, so the results establish benchmark-informed synthetic-to-real transfer more convincingly than generalization to entirely unseen domains.

The parameter study reports no repeated generation/training seeds or uncertainty estimates. This matters particularly for small, inconsistent effects such as lighting augmentation and object-type diversity. Moreover, the assertion that 5,000-image, 75,000-step experiments predict full-scale behavior is not directly validated, and interactions between design choices are largely unexplored.

Several interpretations exceed the controls provided. Adding background furniture changes geometry and occlusion statistics as well as realism, so its benefit does not isolate realistic arrangement as the cause. Similarly, Figure 4 identifies difficult objects and materials, but there is no explicit before/after pruning ablation demonstrating that their removal improves diffuse-region performance. These are plausible explanations rather than established mechanisms.

Reproducibility and comparison details remain incomplete. Training largely defers to original implementations; the sampling weights and training schedule for DLNR-Mixed are not clearly specified. The ETH3D error threshold is omitted from the metric description, and some generation choices, such as the darkness-filter threshold, are unspecified. These omissions make exact reproduction and assessment of the combined-data baseline harder.

Some presentation claims should be qualified. The text says small stereo baselines worsen performance across all benchmarks, whereas Table 1 shows improved ETH3D performance. Table 2's caption also incompletely describes the mixed dataset. These are correctable reporting issues, distinct from the more substantive evaluation concerns above.

strengths: The paper makes a useful empirical and dataset contribution to stereo matching. Its controllable procedural generator enables studies of scene composition, materials, camera baselines, lighting, and rendering cost that are difficult to conduct with fixed synthetic datasets. The contribution is primarily experimental and infrastructural rather than architectural, but is valuable on those terms.

The main dataset improvements are substantial and transfer across architectures. In Table 2, WMGStereo improves over the four-dataset mixture on five of six evaluation columns for RAFT-Stereo, Selective-IGEV, and DLNR, with ETH3D the exception. DLNR's Middlebury 2014 half-resolution error decreases from 5.21 to 3.76, and Booster error from 12.17 to 9.09.

The evaluation includes meaningful controls: matched-model dataset comparisons, three retrained architectures, multiple real-world benchmarks, and additional held-out evaluation. Table 6 strengthens the generalization claim: WMGStereo outperforms all compared training datasets on both Middlebury-Train and DrivingStereo, including FSD. Table 5 also supports the appropriately qualified claim of competitiveness with FSD, rather than universal superiority.

Several ablations provide clear practical guidance. Adding floating objects reduces Middlebury half-resolution error from 12.52 to 6.60, retaining background furniture helps every reported benchmark in that comparison, and narrow baseline ranges produce substantial domain-specific failures. The compute study and appendix further provide useful generation details, including scene reuse, filtering, annotations, and camera sampling.
weaknesses: The causal interpretation of scene realism is stronger than the controls establish. Removing background furniture also changes geometry density, occlusion, and image/depth statistics; comparing indoor scenes with dense floating scenes changes additional factors. These experiments establish that the tested indoor recipe is effective, but do not isolate realistic arrangement itself as the reason.

The parameter study uses one architecture, 5,000 pairs per setting, and 75,000 training steps, without reported repetitions or uncertainty estimates. Consequently, small differences—particularly for lighting and some object/material choices—cannot confidently determine which settings are best. The final dataset's cross-architecture success validates the combined recipe, but does not establish that individual parameter effects persist across architectures or training scales.

The removal of difficult objects and materials lacks a direct downstream ablation. High synthetic per-object or per-material EPE identifies challenging cases, but does not show that excluding them improves generalization. Likewise, the claim that reflective/transparent training harms diffuse regions is not directly tested with material-stratified real-world evaluation; Table 1 reports aggregate benchmark errors.

The sample-efficiency evidence in Figure 5 is limited to DLNR and Middlebury 2014 half-resolution EPE, with no variation across random subsets reported. It supports the stated 500-versus-100,000-example comparison in that setting, but broader claims about dataset saturation and sample efficiency need qualification. Reusing assets across multiple views also makes the unspecified subset-sampling procedure relevant.

Reproducibility is incomplete in the supplied manuscript. The abstract refers to 'this URL,' but the PDF supplies no actual link. Training descriptions largely defer to original-author defaults, without explicitly documenting important comparison settings such as mixture sampling weights, batch sizes, and augmentations. The procedural details are helpful, but the claimed executable release cannot be assessed from this submission.

strengths: The paper provides a useful empirical contribution to stereo training-data design. Its controlled generator enables comparisons of object density, background content, materials, camera baselines, lighting, and rendering cost that are difficult to conduct with fixed datasets. The novelty lies primarily in this analysis and configurable data-generation resource rather than a new stereo architecture.

The strongest evidence is the comparison across three architectures in Table 2. WMGStereo improves over the 600k-pair mixed-data baseline on five of six benchmark columns for RAFT-Stereo, Selective-IGEV, and DLNR, with ETH3D being the exception. For DLNR, Middlebury 2014 half-resolution error decreases from 5.21 to 3.76 and Booster error from 12.17 to 9.09. These substantial, consistent gains support practical usefulness.

Table 6 meaningfully addresses benchmark-driven parameter selection through held-out evaluations. DLNR trained on WMGStereo outperforms all listed training datasets, including FSD, on both error measures for the held-out Middlebury scenes and the 200-pair DrivingStereo subset. Table 5 also supports competitive, though not uniformly superior, performance against FSD under the same architecture.

The generation-cost analysis and supplementary implementation details increase the work's practical value. Table 4 explicitly examines the tradeoff between rendering or arrangement quality and generating more examples. Overall, the supported dataset improvements and actionable analysis favor acceptance despite limitations in the interpretation of individual design choices.
weaknesses: The causal conclusions about realism are stronger than the experimental controls justify. Removing background furniture changes geometry, occlusions, depth distributions, and scene density alongside realism. Likewise, indoor and dense-floating scene types differ in several respects. These experiments establish that particular configurations work better, but do not isolate realistic arrangement as the cause.

Removing difficult objects and materials is insufficiently validated. Figure 3 identifies categories with high synthetic evaluation error, but high error alone does not establish that training on them harms generalization. There is no direct retain-versus-remove ablation or material-specific real-image evaluation supporting the claim that these surfaces degrade performance on diffuse regions. Table 1 actually shows that training with metal and glass improves Booster, underscoring the need to distinguish difficult examples from harmful training examples.

Parameter selection relies on single reported runs using 5k pairs and RAFT-Stereo trained for 75k steps. No repeated generation/training seeds or uncertainty estimates are provided. Large density and baseline effects are persuasive, but smaller differences, particularly for lighting, cannot be confidently interpreted. Final-dataset transfer across architectures does not establish that individual parameter rankings transfer across architectures or training scales.

The sample-efficiency evidence is narrower than the broader scaling discussion suggests: Figure 5 evaluates one architecture on Middlebury 2014 half-resolution EPE with a fixed 200k-step schedule and no uncertainty estimates. It supports an advantage in that setting, but not general sample-efficiency or saturation conclusions across domains.

Reproducibility remains incomplete in the supplied manuscript. The abstract refers to 'this URL' without an actual accessible link, so the claimed code release cannot be assessed. Training details largely defer to original implementations, while the mixed-baseline sampling weights and exact evaluation subset identifiers are unspecified. These omissions matter for a paper whose contribution includes a reproducible generator, although the appendix provides useful generation details.

strengths: The paper makes a useful empirical contribution by systematically studying synthetic stereo data design. Table 1 provides actionable evidence for floating-object density, background geometry, material diversity, and baseline randomization, rather than introducing another dataset without analyzing its construction.

The dataset gains are supported across three architectures under matched training schedules. In Table 2, DLNR improves from 5.21 to 3.76 on Middlebury 2014 (H) and from 12.17 to 9.09 on Booster relative to training on the four-dataset mixture. RAFT-Stereo and Selective-IGEV show broadly consistent improvements.

Held-out evaluation strengthens the generalization evidence: Table 6 reports improvements over both the mixed baseline and FSD on additional Middlebury scenes and DrivingStereo. Table 5 also supports competitiveness with FSD, although neither dataset wins consistently.

The generation-cost analysis is practically valuable. Table 4 evaluates rendering and scene-solver simplifications, including a generation-compute-matched comparison. The appendix documents camera placement, annotations, filtering, and scene construction.

Overall, the substantial dataset utility and informative controlled experiments support weak acceptance. A new architecture or uniformly best benchmark performance is unnecessary for this contribution.

Removing background furniture also changes geometry density, occlusion, and disparity statistics; comparing indoor and dense-floating scenes changes several factors simultaneously. These experiments establish useful generation recipes more clearly than an independent benefit from realistic arrangement.

Figure 3 identifies high-error assets, but there is no explicit before/after removal ablation or material-stratified real-world evaluation. The all-metal/glass experiment changes the entire training distribution and cannot isolate the effect of removing particular problematic materials.

Parameter selection relies on single reported 5,000-pair, 75k-step RAFT-Stereo experiments, without uncertainty estimates or repeated generation/training seeds. Large density and baseline effects are persuasive, but small lighting and material differences are less conclusive. Cross-architecture validation of the final dataset does not establish that individual parameter rankings transfer.

Reproducibility is incomplete in the supplied manuscript: the abstract refers to 'this URL' without an actual link, and the mixed-dataset sampling weights and exact training configurations are insufficiently specified. The procedural description is helpful, but the claimed code release cannot be verified from the submission.
